title: How to Build a Home Inventory for Insurance, Room by Room
seo_title: Home Inventory for Insurance: A Room-by-Room Guide
meta_description: Build a home inventory for insurance that holds up at claim time: a room-by-room checklist, photo and video tips, receipts and storage.
body_html:
After a fire, burglary, or burst pipe, your insurer will usually ask you to list what you lost, often item by item. Trying to remember everything in a stressful moment is hard, and whatever you forget, you generally do not get paid for. A home inventory done ahead of time solves that, and it takes less effort than most people think.

This guide works for renters and homeowners alike. It is general information, not insurance or legal advice, and every policy has its own documentation requirements.

Why a home inventory matters

A good inventory helps you in three ways:

  • Faster, smoother claims. You can hand your adjuster a list with photos instead of rebuilding your memory from scratch.
  • Better coverage decisions. Once you see the total value of what you own, you can check whether your personal property limit is high enough.
  • Proof of ownership and condition. Photos, receipts, and serial numbers support the value you claim and can help after a theft, too.

If you are not sure what your policy covers in the first place, start with what renters insurance covers. Homeowners policies follow a similar structure for personal property.

What to record for each item

You do not need every detail for every spoon. Focus your effort on items that would be costly or hard to replace. For those, try to capture:

DetailWhy it helps
Description, brand, and modelLets the adjuster price a comparable replacement
Serial numberSupports ownership and helps police after a theft
Approximate purchase dateUsed to estimate depreciation
Purchase price or estimated valueGives a starting point for the claim
Photo or videoShows the item existed and its condition
Receipt, appraisal, or order confirmationStrongest proof of value, especially for high-value items

Give high-value items extra attention

Jewelry, watches, art, collectibles, firearms, and specialty electronics often have lower coverage limits under a standard policy. For these, keep appraisals or receipts with your inventory and ask your agent whether a scheduled personal property endorsement makes sense. Seeing the full list in one place is often what prompts people to ask that question for the first time.

For everyday items like clothing, books, and kitchenware, a photo of the open closet or cabinet plus a rough count is usually enough to jog your memory later.

Step by step: how to create your inventory

  1. Pick your tool. A simple spreadsheet, a notes app, a dedicated home inventory app, or a printed checklist all work. The best tool is the one you will actually finish.
  2. Start with one room. Do not try to do the whole house in a day. One room per evening is a realistic pace.
  3. Record a walkthrough video. Narrate as you go: "Living room, 65-inch TV, bought about two years ago." Open drawers, closets, and cabinets.
  4. Take close-up photos of valuable items, labels, and serial number plates.
  5. Add the details from the table above for anything costly.
  6. Gather proof of value. Search your email and online store accounts for order confirmations. Snap photos of paper receipts before they fade.
  7. Back it all up off-site (more on that below).
  8. Set a reminder to update it.

Room-by-room checklist

Use this as a prompt list so you do not overlook whole categories.

Living room

  • TV, streaming devices, sound system, gaming consoles and games
  • Sofa, chairs, tables, rugs, lamps
  • Artwork, décor, books, media collections

Kitchen and dining

  • Small appliances: mixer, blender, coffee maker, air fryer, microwave
  • Cookware, knives, dishes, glassware, flatware
  • Dining table and chairs, pantry stock
  • For homeowners: refrigerator, range, dishwasher (note make and model)

Bedrooms

  • Mattresses, bed frames, dressers, nightstands
  • Clothing, shoes, coats, handbags (photograph closets with doors open)
  • Jewelry and watches (close-ups, plus appraisals if you have them)

Bathrooms

  • Towels and linens, hair tools, electric toothbrushes, scales
  • Toiletries and cosmetics add up more than you might think

Home office

  • Computers, monitors, printers, phones, tablets, cameras
  • Desk, chair, shelving, external drives
  • Note any business equipment separately, since many personal policies limit it

Garage, closets, and storage

  • Tools, ladders, lawn equipment, bikes, sports gear
  • Holiday decorations, camping gear, luggage
  • Items in a storage unit (check how your policy treats off-site storage)

Photo and video tips that make a difference

  • Use good light and shoot wide first, then close-up.
  • Show brand labels and model tags, which are often on the back or bottom.
  • Keep the original files. Phone photos usually carry a date stamp in their file data, which helps show when the photo was taken.
  • Capture condition. A clear shot of a well-kept item helps if depreciation is discussed later.
  • Do not forget the structure if you own your home: flooring, cabinets, fixtures, and upgrades. Those photos can help with dwelling claims too.

Where to store your inventory

An inventory kept only on a laptop in the house can be lost in the same fire or flood it was meant to document. Keep at least one copy off-site:

  • A cloud storage account or the backup built into your inventory app
  • An email to yourself with the spreadsheet and a link to the photo folder
  • A USB drive at a relative's home, at work, or in a safe deposit box
  • Paper copies of key receipts and appraisals in a fire- and water-resistant pouch

It also helps to store a copy of your insurance policy and declarations page in the same place, along with your insurer's claim phone number.

Keep it current without a big project

  • Add big purchases the day you unbox them: snap a photo and save the receipt.
  • Do a quick review once a year. Some people tie it to a memorable date, like the policy renewal.
  • Update after moving, remodeling, or receiving valuable gifts.
  • Recheck your coverage limits whenever your total grows noticeably.

Using your inventory when you file a claim

If you have a loss, your inventory becomes the backbone of your claim:

  1. Report the claim and ask the adjuster what format they want for the contents list.
  2. Mark which items were damaged or lost and photograph the damage.
  3. Do not throw away damaged items until the adjuster says it is OK, unless they create a safety hazard. If you must, photograph them first.
  4. Keep a copy of everything you send, and check your policy for notice and proof-of-loss deadlines.

Contents claims after large losses can get complicated. If the numbers are far apart, read about how public adjusters help with insurance claims and the insurance appraisal process. The Insurance Information Institute also offers consumer resources on home inventories.

Frequently asked questions

Is a video enough for a home inventory?

A narrated video is a great start and far better than nothing. Adding a written list with serial numbers and values for expensive items makes it much stronger.

What if I do not have receipts?

Photos, bank or card statements, online order history, owner's manuals, and even photos of the item in the background of family pictures can help support ownership and value.

How long does a home inventory take?

It depends on your home, but spreading it out one room at a time keeps it manageable. A quick video walkthrough can be done in a single session.

Should renters make an inventory too?

Yes. Renters often own more than they realize, and an inventory helps you choose the right coverage limit and file a complete claim.

Have a system that works for you, or a lesson learned from a past claim? Share it in our Insurance Claims community so other renters and homeowners can learn from it. For help with a specific claim, your insurer, a licensed public adjuster, or an attorney can advise you.
